patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral eyelid drooping and double vision with breathlessness on exertion
patient.hpi:
A 68-year-old British man with no significant prior medical history presented to the neurology ward with a 5-month history of bilateral eyelid drooping and double vision. He first noticed right upper eyelid ptosis that gradually progressed to complete closure over approximately 10 days, followed 6 weeks later by left-sided ptosis and periorbital puffiness. Both eyes exhibited restricted extraocular movements in all directions. He also reported shortness of breath when walking a short distance — previously able to walk a mile without difficulty but now dyspneic after climbing one flight of stairs. He denied diplopia at rest (as vision was fully obstructed by ptosis), dysphagia, difficulty chewing, or limb weakness. There was no history of hypertension, diabetes, or malignancy. He had no smoking history and took no medications. His family history was unremarkable for neuromuscular or autoimmune conditions.

On examination, there was complete bilateral ptosis with restricted extraocular movements in all planes. The ice pack test applied to each eyelid for 5 minutes produced a 3–4 mm improvement in ptosis bilaterally, a positive result. Bulbar muscle testing demonstrated fatigable palate elevation consistent with the SLURP test. Limb strength was 5/5 throughout with preserved reflexes and sensation. Auscultation revealed mildly decreased breath sounds at the right base. A chest radiograph performed in the emergency department showed an oval, well-defined radio-opaque lesion in the right hemithorax adjacent to the anterior mediastinum. The radiograph was flagged by the radiographer but was initially attributed by the admitting team to possible lymphoma or germ cell tumor rather than thymoma — the connection to an underlying neuromuscular process was not immediately made.

family_history: No family history of neuromuscular or autoimmune disease

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive, generalized (MGFA Class IIb)

differential.key_features: Imaging cannot definitively distinguish; tissue diagnosis required.
Lobulated anterior mediastinal mass differential includes lymphoma; tissue diagnosis discriminates.
Smoker risk for SCLC; here AChR positive and CT shows discrete thymoma, not lung lesion.
Anterior mediastinal mass differential in younger patients; less likely at 68 without elevated tumor markers.
No MRI findings; fluctuating fatigable pattern incompatible with focal lesion.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR antibody positive; TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

tool_parameters.query: myasthenia gravis MGFA classification treatment thymectomy

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, procainamide)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Flag aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, telithromycin, NMBs as contraindicated or use-with-caution in MG

optimal_actions.action: Bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) — repeat q4h in crisis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline FVC/NIF to assess crisis risk in patients with bulbar or limb involvement

optimal_actions.action: Bedside ice-pack test for ptosis (cheap, ~80% sensitive for ocular MG)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Improvement of ptosis after 2 minutes of cooling supports MG

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: Thoracic surgery referral for thymoma resection (Masaoka staging)
Pre-thymectomy MG optimization with pyridostigmine + IVIG or PLEX
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Anti-titin or anti-RyR antibodies in an MG patient strongly predict thymoma — CT chest is mandatory and surgical referral is non-negotiable.

red_herrings.finding: Anterior mediastinal mass initially evaluated as lymphoma or germ cell tumor
red_herrings.why_misleading: Admitting team focused on oncological differential without connecting mediastinal mass to bilateral ptosis and ophthalmoplegia
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anterior mediastinal mass + bilateral ptosis + positive ice pack test = thymoma-associated MG; MG antibody panel is the key next step

red_herrings.finding: Age 68 with bilateral ptosis — CPEO in differential
red_herrings.why_misleading: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia is a mitochondrial disorder with bilateral ptosis and ophthalmoplegia mimicking MG
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Positive ice pack test, anti-titin positivity, and thymoma on CT distinguish MG from CPEO

red_herrings.why_misleading: Could suggest thyroid ophthalmopathy; Graves' disease is common in elderly males with bilateral eye changes
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal TSH, normal orbital MRI (no EOM enlargement, no proptosis), and ptosis (not lid retraction) exclude thyroid ophthalmopathy

additional_observations:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

Indication: Anterior mediastinal mass on chest radiograph and partially visualized on brain MRI; bilateral ptosis and extraocular restriction requiring etiologic investigation

TECHNIQUE: Multi-detector CT chest with IV contrast, 1mm reconstructions, mediastinal and lung windows

FINDINGS:
ANTERIOR MEDIASTINUM:
  Well-defined, lobulated, oval soft-tissue density mass in the anterior mediastinum, predominantly right-sided, measuring 4.4 × 3.2 × 3.8 cm. The mass has homogeneous soft-tissue density (40 HU pre-contrast, 95 HU post-contrast with uniform enhancement). No calcification, cystic component, fat component, or necrosis. The mass partially obliterates the retrosternal space and abuts but does not invade the right atrial border or great vessels. No pericardial effusion.

PLEURAL SPACES: No effusion. No pneumothorax.

LUNG PARENCHYMA: No consolidation, masses, or ground-glass opacities.

LYMPH NODES: No pathologically enlarged mediastinal or hilar lymph nodes.

BONES: No lytic or sclerotic lesions.

IMPRESSION:
1. Well-defined anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass (4.4 cm), uniformly enhancing without fat or calcification, abutting the right cardiac border without invasion. Appearance is most consistent with thymoma (WHO classification pending histology). Thymic carcinoma and lymphoma are in the differential but less favored given absence of adenopathy and homogeneous enhancement.
2. No pleural, pericardial, or pulmonary metastatic disease.

RECOMMENDATION: Surgical or pathological evaluation recommended for tissue characterization. Clinical correlation with neuromuscular findings recommended.
ct.impression: CT chest with contrast: Well-defined lobulated anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass (4.4 × 3.2 × 3.8 cm), uniformly enhancing, without calcification, fat, cystic change, or necrosis. The mass abuts the right cardiac border without imaging evidence of invasion. No pathologically enlarged mediastinal or hilar lymph nodes. No pleural effusion or pulmonary parenchymal disease. Imaging appearances are most consistent with a primary thymic neoplasm. Tissue diagnosis recommended for histological characterization. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG — ORBICULARIS OCULI

Indication: Bilateral ptosis; neuromuscular junction assessment

RESULTS:
  Mean consecutive difference (MCD): 62 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
  Blocking: 22% of potential pairs showed intermittent blocking
  Fiber density: 1.9 (normal ≤2.0)

INTERPRETATION: Markedly increased jitter (MCD 62 µs; reference <35 µs) with 22% blocking rate. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

CONCLUSION: Abnormal SFEMG. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: Confirm NMJ dysfunction; pre-operative assessment for thymectomy

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS at orbicularis oculi, nasalis, trapezius

RESULTS:
  Orbicularis oculi: Decrement 20% (1st to 4th stimulus) [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Nasalis: Decrement 17% ABNORMAL
  Trapezius: Decrement 12% ABNORMAL

CONCLUSION: Significant abnormal decremental response in multiple muscle groups. Findings indicate a generalized disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Clinical literature
results.content:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Thymoma-Associated Myasthenia Gravis — Management

KEY EVIDENCE:
1. MGTX TRIAL (Wolfe GI et al., NEJM 2016): Thymectomy improves outcomes in AChR+ generalized MG patients 18-65 even without thymoma. For thymoma-associated MG, thymectomy is universally recommended (regardless of age) for oncologic control.

2. THYMOMA HISTOLOGY (WHO Classification):
   - Type A, AB, B1, B2, B3 thymoma (Type B associated with higher MG risk)
   - Masaoka staging used for prognosis
   - CT appearances: encapsulated (A/AB/B1), more lobulated (B2/B3)

3. PRE-OPERATIVE OPTIMIZATION:
   - IVIG or PLEX 2-4 weeks before thymectomy to reduce crisis risk
   - Pyridostigmine dose adjusted; may need to hold on morning of surgery
   - Prolonged ventilator dependency post-op is common in bulbar MG

4. ANTI-TITIN ANTIBODIES:
   - Marker for thymoma in AChR+ MG; high specificity in patients <60 years
   - Also associated with severe MG phenotype and higher rate of myasthenic crisis

CONCLUSION: Thymoma-associated MG has both neurological and oncological implications; interdisciplinary evaluation including neurology and thoracic surgery is standard of care. Pre-operative neuromuscular status assessment is recommended.

output.summary: Evidence supports thymectomy for AChR-positive generalized MG with thymoma for both oncological and neurological indications. Anti-titin antibody positivity is associated with thymoma in AChR-positive MG. Pre-operative assessment of neuromuscular status is recommended. Multidisciplinary approach is standard of care.

interactions:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — PYRIDOSTIGMINE IN MG

Query: Pyridostigmine interactions and initiation in newly diagnosed MG

FINDINGS:
  PYRIDOSTIGMINE (AChE inhibitor, 60 mg q4-6h standard):
  - Excessive dosing → cholinergic crisis: monitor for muscarinic side effects (diarrhea, hypersalivation, bradycardia)
  - Beta-blockers (e.g., atenolol, metoprolol): enhance bradycardia risk with pyridostigmine — use with caution
  - Atropine is antidote for cholinergic crisis
  - Anticholinergic medications (antihistamines, TCAs): may antagonize pyridostigmine effect
  - No thymoma-specific drug interactions; however, immunosuppressants (prednisone, azathioprine, mycophenolate) typically added after thymectomy if symptoms persist

STARTING DOSE FOR NEW MG:
  Pyridostigmine 30-60 mg orally every 4-6 hours; titrate to symptom relief
  For bulbar symptoms: use liquid formulation (Mestinon Syrup)

CONCLUSION: Pyridostigmine has a well-characterized interaction profile; excessive dosing may produce cholinergic effects. Concurrent anticholinergic or beta-blocking agents warrant monitoring. Clinical correlation and prescriber guidance recommended.
warnings: Pyridostigmine: monitor for cholinergic excess (bradycardia, hypersalivation, diarrhea); beta-adrenergic blocking agents may enhance bradycardia risk.
